title: Pie charts, histograms, dot plots and stem-and-leaf plots
blurb: Turn pie-chart percents and angles into amounts, count across histogram intervals, and read every value off a dot plot or stem-and-leaf plot.
question: A pie chart of 600 clinic visits shows a 'Sports physicals' slice with a central angle of 252°. A histogram beside it groups patient ages into intervals. How many visits were sports physicals, and what can and can't you say about exact ages from the histogram?

teach.h: Parts of a whole, or how values spread
teach.body: Formally, a pie (circle) chart shows each category as a percent of one whole, while histograms, dot plots and stem-and-leaf plots show the distribution of numerical data. In plain English: a pie chart answers 'what share?', and the other three answer 'how many values landed where?' Dot plots and stem-and-leaf plots keep every individual value; a histogram groups values into intervals and loses the exact numbers.

teach.h: Marcus's $2,400 monthly budget as a pie chart
head: Slice
Percent
Central angle
Amount
teach.caption: Percents sum to 100%, angles to 360°, amounts to the total. If they don't, the chart is wrong or you misread it.

items: Amount = percent × total. Food: 0.15 × $2,400 = $360. Check: $360 ÷ $2,400 = 0.15. ✓
Central angle = percent × 360°. Rent: 0.40 × 360° = 144°. Check: 144 ÷ 360 = 0.4. ✓
Angle back to percent: a 54° slice is 54 ÷ 360 = 0.15 = 15%.
Missing slice: 100% − (40% + 25% + 15% + 10%) = 10% for Other.
Reverse: if you only knew Rent was $960 and 40%, the total is $960 ÷ 0.40 = $2,400.

teach.h: Histogram data: ages of 50 clinic patients
teach.caption: On a real histogram the bars stand upright and TOUCH, because the intervals run on without gaps. Each bar's height is a frequency (a count), not an age.

items: Patients aged 40 or older: 18 + 9 + 3 = 30. As a percent: 30 ÷ 50 = 60%.
Check the total first: 6 + 14 + 18 + 9 + 3 = 50. ✓
Which interval holds the median? With 50 values, the median is between the 25th and 26th. Running totals: 6, then 20, then 38. Both fall in 40–59.
What you CANNOT say: how many patients are exactly 45, or the oldest patient's age. The histogram only gives counts per interval.

teach.h: Dot plot: ER visits last year by 20 patients
teach.caption: Each dot is one patient. The value is the position on the axis; the number of dots is how many patients had it.

teach.h: Worked example: statistics from the dot plot
items: Count the dots: 7 + 6 + 4 + 2 + 0 + 1 = 20 patients.
Median: the 10th and 11th values. The first 7 values are 0 and values 8 to 13 are 1, so both are 1. Median = 1.
Mode = 0 (the tallest stack). Range = 5 − 0 = 5.

head: Stem (tens)
Leaves (ones)
teach.caption: Key: 6 | 2 = 62 beats per minute. Always read the key: on another plot 6 | 2 could mean 6.2.

teach.h: Worked example: reading the stem-and-leaf plot
items: Median: the 8th of 15 values = 71.
Mode: 73 (three leaves of 3 on stem 7).
Range: 91 − 58 = 33. Rates above 75: 78, 82, 85 and 91, so 4 patients.

teach.text: Classic slips: using a pie chart's percent (or its angle) as the amount; reading a histogram bar as one exact value; taking the mode of a dot plot when the mean was asked; and ignoring the stem-and-leaf key, so 7 | 4 read as 74 when the key says 7.4.

items: Pie: amount = percent × total; angle = percent × 360°; percent = angle ÷ 360.
Histogram: bars touch, x-axis = intervals, height = frequency; add bars for 'at least' or 'fewer than'.
Dot plot: each dot is one value; multiply value × dots to find the sum.
Stem-and-leaf: stem + leaf = value per the key; the values are already in order.

summary: You can now convert pie-chart percents and central angles into amounts and back, count and locate the median interval on a histogram, and calculate mean, median, mode and range straight from a dot plot or stem-and-leaf plot. You also know which displays keep exact values and which do not.

A.q: A pie chart shows the reasons for 600 visits to a campus health center. The 'Sports physicals' slice has a central angle of 252°. How many visits were sports physicals?

whyNot.0: 70 is the percent of the whole, not the number of visits.
whyNot.1: 180 is 30% of 600, the rest of the chart rather than this slice.
whyNot.2: 252 is the central angle in degrees, not a count of visits.

A.q: A histogram shows emergency department wait times for 60 patients: 0–14 min: 9; 15–29 min: 21; 30–44 min: 16; 45–59 min: 10; 60–74 min: 4. How many patients waited less than 45 minutes?
A.why: Less than 45 minutes covers 0–14, 15–29 and 30–44: 9 + 21 + 16 = 46. Check: 60 − (10 + 4) = 46.

whyNot.0: 16 is the 30–44 bar alone, not every interval below 45.

A.q: A dot plot shows how many prescriptions each of 15 patients filled last month: 1 (2 dots), 2 (5 dots), 3 (4 dots), 4 (3 dots), 6 (1 dot). What is the mean number of prescriptions per patient?

whyNot.1: 3 is the median (the 8th of 15 values), not the mean.
whyNot.2: 3.2 averages the five axis values (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6) ÷ 5, ignoring how many dots each has.
whyNot.3: 3.5 is halfway between the lowest and highest values, not the mean.

B.q: A stem-and-leaf plot shows fasting blood glucose in mg/dL (key: 8 | 4 = 84). 7 | 6 8 9; 8 | 2 4 4 7; 9 | 0 3 5 5 5 8; 10 | 1 6; 11 | 4. What is the median?
B.why: There are 3 + 4 + 6 + 2 + 1 = 16 values, so the median is the mean of the 8th and 9th. In order: 76, 78, 79, 82, 84, 84, 87, 90, 93, ... The 8th is 90 and the 9th is 93: (90 + 93) ÷ 2 = 91.5.

whyNot.0: 90 is the 8th value alone. With an even count, average the two middle values.
whyNot.2: 93 is the 9th value alone. With an even count, average the two middle values.
whyNot.3: 95 is the mode (it appears three times), not the median.

B.q: A histogram shows 40 applicants' practice test scores: 50–59: 4; 60–69: 10; 70–79: 15; 80–89: 8; 90–99: 3. Which statement must be true?
B.why: Scores of 70 or higher: 15 + 8 + 3 = 26, and 26 is more than half of 40. Every other statement needs exact values the histogram does not show.

whyNot.1: The median lies in the 70–79 interval, but the histogram cannot show that it is exactly 75.
whyNot.2: Three applicants scored somewhere from 90 to 99; none has to be exactly 99.
whyNot.3: Fifteen applicants scored from 70 to 79. The bar does not say any scored exactly 79.

B.q: A pie chart of Ms. Ortiz's monthly budget shows rent as a 35% slice. Her rent is $840. What is her total monthly budget?

whyNot.1: $840 × 3.5 = $2,940 multiplies instead of dividing and misplaces the decimal.
whyNot.2: $840 ÷ 0.035 = $24,000 moves the decimal three places instead of two.
whyNot.3: $840 × 35 = $29,400 multiplies by the percent as a whole number.

C.q: A pie chart shows how 720 students prepare for the TEAS: App 40%, Book 25%, Class (central angle 81°) and Tutor (the remaining slice). How many students chose a tutor?

whyNot.0: 81 is the Class slice's angle in degrees, not a number of students.
whyNot.2: 0.225 × 720 = 162 is the number who chose a class, not a tutor.

C.q: A histogram shows the systolic blood pressure of 40 patients: 100–109: 12; 110–119: 10; 120–129: 4; 130–139: 6; 140–149: 8. Which interval contains the median?
C.why: With 40 values the median is between the 20th and 21st. Running totals: 12 after 100–109, then 22 after 110–119. The 20th and 21st values both fall in 110–119.

whyNot.0: 100–109 is the tallest bar, which locates the modal interval, not the median.
whyNot.2: 120–129 is the middle interval on the axis, but only 4 values sit there; the running total has passed 20 before it.
whyNot.3: 130–139 is past the halfway point: 26 values are already below it.

C.q: A stem-and-leaf plot shows 12 newborn weights in pounds (key: 7 | 4 = 7.4 lb). 5 | 9; 6 | 2 8; 7 | 1 4 4 6 9; 8 | 0 3 5; 9 | 7. What is the mean weight? Round to the nearest tenth.

whyNot.0: 7.4 is the mode, the weight that appears twice.
whyNot.3: 75.7 ignores the key and reads 7 | 4 as 74 instead of 7.4.

reteach.title: A pizza and a coat check
reteach.question: Think of a pizza cut for friends, and a coat check that sorts coats onto numbered racks. Which one is a pie chart, and which is a histogram?

blocks.body: A pie chart is a pizza: the whole pie is 100% (and 360°), and each slice is a share. If the pizza cost $20 and your slice is 25%, your share is 0.25 × $20 = $5. A histogram is a coat check sorting coats by size: rack '30–39' holds 8 coats, but you can't tell which exact size each coat is without opening the rack. A dot plot or stem-and-leaf plot is a coat check that writes every coat's exact size on a tag.

blocks.text: A slice's percent is not the amount. A 25% slice of a 600-patient chart is 0.25 × 600 = 150 patients, not 25.

explain.body: The whole circle is 100% and 360°. Amount = percent × total; angle = percent × 360°; percent = angle ÷ 360. A missing slice is 100% minus the others.

test.q: A clinic's supply budget pie chart has slices of 25%, 30% and 15%, and one more slice labeled 'Other.' What is the central angle of the Other slice?

whyNot.0: 30° uses the percent as the angle without multiplying by 360.
whyNot.1: 90° is the angle of the 25% slice.
whyNot.3: 252° is the angle of the three named slices combined (70% of 360°).

explain.body: A histogram groups numerical data into equal, touching intervals. The height of each bar is a frequency. To count 'at least' or 'fewer than' a value, add the whole bars on that side; exact values inside a bar are unknown.

test.q: A histogram shows the hospital stays of 30 patients: 1–2 days: 11; 3–4 days: 9; 5–6 days: 6; 7–8 days: 4. What percent of the patients stayed 4 days or fewer? Round to the nearest tenth of a percent.

whyNot.1: 33.3% is the complement: patients who stayed 5 days or more (10 ÷ 30).

explain.body: Each dot is one data value, stacked above its number on the axis. Sum = value × number of dots, added across the plot. Mean = sum ÷ total dots. The tallest stack is the mode.

test.q: A dot plot shows practice tests taken by 12 students: 1 (2 dots), 2 (4 dots), 3 (3 dots), 4 (1 dot), 6 (2 dots). What is the mean number of practice tests? Round to the nearest tenth.

whyNot.0: 2 is the mode (the tallest stack), not the mean.
whyNot.1: 2.5 is the median: the 6th value is 2 and the 7th is 3.
whyNot.3: 3.2 averages the axis values (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 6) ÷ 5, ignoring the dot counts.

explain.body: Each leaf joins its stem to make one value, as the key shows (3 | 6 = 36). The leaves are in order, so count to the middle for the median. With an even count, average the two middle values.

test.q: A stem-and-leaf plot shows the ages of 10 blood donors (key: 3 | 6 = 36). 2 | 5 8; 3 | 0 1 4 6 9; 4 | 2 7; 5 | 3. What is the median age?
test.why: Ordered: 25, 28, 30, 31, 34, 36, 39, 42, 47, 53. With 10 values, average the 5th and 6th: (34 + 36) ÷ 2 = 35.

whyNot.0: 34 is the 5th value alone; with an even count you average the 5th and 6th.
whyNot.2: 36 is the 6th value alone; with an even count you average the 5th and 6th.
whyNot.3: 36.5 is the mean (365 ÷ 10), not the median.
